chunks: What is a current probe. The question: What is a current probe?
A current probe measures the current in a wire without cutting it. You clamp the probe around the wire, and it senses the magnetic field the current creates.
It sends the scope a voltage proportional to the current, such as 10 millivolts per amp. There is no resistor in the circuit, and the probe has no electrical connection to it.
A compass needle near a wire swings because current makes a magnetic field around it. More current, bigger swing.
A current probe is a precise compass wrapped around the wire, measuring the field instead of the current itself.
One catch: around two wires carrying equal and opposite currents, the fields cancel.
A current transformer works like a high-pass filter. Above f L the output follows the current; below it the response falls 20 decibels/decade, so DC is lost and slow pulses droop.
This is why a pure CT probe cannot see DC offset or the flat top of a long pulse. Drag L up to 0. 5 henries and f L falls to about 1.
6 hertz, so long pulses droop far less; a 50 ohms burden with the default 10 millihenries pushes f L up to about 800 hertz.
Magnetic field: the invisible influence around a current-carrying wire. Its strength is proportional to the current. Sensitivity: the output per amp, in mV/A.
Transformer-type (AC) probe: reads only changing current, not steady DC. Hall-effect probe: uses a small sensor that responds to a steady field, so it can read DC as well as AC.
Noise floor: the smallest current the probe can show above its own noise.
A probe has a sensitivity of 10 millivolts per amp. You clamp it around one wire of a motor cable, and the scope shows a waveform peaking at 50 millivolts.
The current peaks at 50 over 10 equals 5 amps. Now suppose you clamp around both the supply and return wires.
The currents are equal and opposite, so the net current inside the clamp is zero, and the probe reads about 0 amps. Clamp one wire only.
For DC, such as a battery current, you need a Hall-effect probe, and you must zero it before use. A transformer-type probe cannot see a steady current. That is the whole idea.
"A current probe senses the magnetic field around a wire so I can see current without breaking the circuit or adding a series resistor.
An AC probe is a clamp-on transformer, a Hall-effect probe adds DC capability, and a Rogowski coil is an air-cored coil giving di/dt that is integrated.
I zero or degauss it, clamp one conductor with the arrow along the current, and watch bandwidth, saturation and noise floor.
For tiny currents I wind extra turns through the clamp."
Quick check. You clamp a current probe around a two-wire power cable (supply and return) carrying 5 amps. What does it read?
